concepts.definition: A short text that clearly writes down the results, the mistakes and the limits of reliability.
concepts.example: It gives the accuracy, the per-label results, the wrong cases, an idea for improvement and how far it can be trusted.
concepts.pitfall: Writing only "accuracy 80%" and leaving out the mistakes and the limits.

concepts.definition: The number of cases needed to trust a result; the fewer there are, the more the result jumps around.
concepts.example: In a set of 10 cases, a single case moves the accuracy by 10 points.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the result of a small set is certain.

concepts.definition: A case where the system is likely to go wrong, and which exposes a weak point.
concepts.example: In the sentence `Hata yok` (No errors), `hata` (error) is a word in the negative list; the system says negative.
concepts.pitfall: Avoiding hard cases to try to make the system look good.

concepts.definition: Running the eval again after changing the system to see that the earlier success is kept.
concepts.example: When you add a new word, you check whether the old cases still pass.
concepts.pitfall: Not running the eval again after a fix; you might break one thing while fixing another.

concepts.definition: The cases used to improve the system, and the cases kept aside to measure the final success.
concepts.example: You fix the rule with the first 10 cases and report the final accuracy with a separate 10 cases.
concepts.pitfall: Keeping the two the same; the measurement comes out too optimistic.

quiz.prompt: In a set of 10 cases, the system shows 80% accuracy. If one more case in the set had come out wrong, by how many percentage points would the accuracy have dropped?
quiz.explanation: With 10 cases, each case is worth 10%: 8/10 = 80%, 7/10 = 70%. A single case moves it by 10 points. In a set of 100 cases the same difference would be 1 point; that is why the results of small sets are viewed with caution.

quiz.prompt: Which of these report sentences is the most honest?
options: I got 75% accuracy on 12 cases; the set is small, so the result is not certain. The mistakes are concentrated in sarcastic sentences.
I removed the hard cases, so the accuracy became 100%.
The system works; there is no need to test it.
quiz.explanation: A good report gives the number, the size of the set and where the mistakes are concentrated, all together. Removing the hard cases improves the measurement falsely; and saying "perfect" cannot be backed up by a single number.

quiz.prompt:
The sentiment classifier looks at word lists; `hata` (error) and `kullanışsız` (useless) are in the negative list, `hızlı` (fast) is in the positive list, and `yok` (none) is in no list. `değil` (not) flips the previous score; if the score is 0, "unclear". A set of six cases is run:

```
("Çok iyi"                 , positive)
("Kolay değil"             , negative)
("Toplantı saat beşte"     , unclear)
("Süper ama zor"           , unclear)
("Hızlı ve kullanışsız"    , negative)
("Hata yok"                , positive)
```

Which cases are got wrong?
options: The 5th case, "fast and useless", and the 6th case, "no errors"; accuracy 4/6
The 4th case, "great but hard", and the 2nd case, "not easy"; accuracy 4/6
quiz.explanation: "Fast and useless": +1 and -1 add up to 0, the system says unclear; the expected label is negative. "No errors": "error" -1, "none" is in no list, the system says negative; the expected label is positive. The other four cases are correct ("Great but hard": +1 and -1, unclear; "Not easy": negative). Accuracy 4/6, about 67%.

quiz.prompt:
A student measures their system with the steps below. Which line has the mistake that makes the measurement too optimistic?

```
1: vakalar = yaz(10)
2: kurali_ayarla(vakalar)      # fix the rule to suit these cases
3: skor = olc(vakalar)         # measure with the same cases
4: rapor_yaz(skor)
```
options: Line 3: the measurement is done with the cases used for tuning; a separate set is needed
Line 2: the rule should not be tuned at all
Line 4: the report should not be written
quiz.explanation: Because the rule was fitted to these cases on line 2, the score on line 3 comes out better than it is (data leakage). The solution is to keep separate sets for tuning and for measurement. Tuning the rule and writing a report are not wrong.

quiz.prompt: Why do you run the eval again every time you change the system?
options: To see whether a fix has broken other cases
So that the accuracy always stays the same
It is not needed, because the eval runs by itself
quiz.explanation: Adding a word can fix one mistake while breaking another case. Running the eval after every change (a regression test) shows this straight away. Keeping the accuracy fixed is not the aim; the aim is to measure the truth.
